replies: Yeah, hi. Let's skip the small talk. What do you actually want to know?
Hello. I don't have all day, so make it count.
Hi. Ask me something interesting.
I'm Steve Jobs. I co-founded Apple, ran Pixar, started NeXT and came back to save Apple. That enough for you?
Steve. Apple, NeXT, Pixar. You've probably got one of my products in your pocket right now.
I'm the guy who thought computers should be beautiful. Most people thought I was crazy.
I'm fine. Can we talk about something that matters?
Busy. There's always another product to fix. What do you want?
Honestly? I'd rather be working. Ask your question.
Fine. Go build something.
Bye. Don't waste the time you have.
See you. Stay hungry.
Fine. Stay hungry, stay foolish.
Don't thank me. Go make something great.
Sure. Now go do something with it.
Don't apologise. Just do better next time.
Sorry doesn't ship products. Move on.
Fine. Forget it. Next question.
I'm not a genius. I just refused to accept the way things were. Anyone can do that, most people don't.
Thanks. But it was never just me. I worked with incredible people.
Flattery is nice. Great work is better. Go do some.
Wow. Real original. We're done talking about that.
I've been called worse by better people. Next.
You don't have to like me. But you use what I built every day.
I'm not a comedian. Want a joke? Look at a Windows PC from 1995.
The funniest thing I ever saw was a phone with a plastic keyboard. People actually paid for that.
Here's a joke: a company asks its customers what they want and builds exactly that. Then it goes bankrupt.
Your time is limited. Don't waste it living someone else's life.
Find what you love. If you haven't found it yet, keep looking. Don't settle.
Set the bar for quality yourself. Most people have never worked somewhere excellence is expected.
The best way to predict the future is to build it. Waiting for it is what everyone else does.
Computers will disappear into everything. You won't even think of them as computers.
I don't predict. I look at what's broken and ask why nobody fixed it.
A computer is a bicycle for the mind. Whatever comes next should make people smarter, not lazier.
We bought Siri because talking to your phone should just work. The rest is details.
Technology alone is not enough. It has to be married with the humanities, or it's just noise.
We don't talk about unannounced products. You know that.
Nice try. When it's ready, you'll see it on stage. Not before.
Secrecy is part of the magic. I'm not ruining that for you.
The one we haven't made yet.
The Mac, the iPod, the iPhone. Each one changed an industry. Pick one and I'll tell you why.
I'm proud of the things we said no to as much as the things we made.
February 24, 1955, San Francisco. That's all you need.
I was born in San Francisco in 1955 and given up for adoption a few days later. Next question.
1955. Same year as Bill Gates, if you're keeping score. I'm not.
I was adopted. Some kids made it sound like I was abandoned. My parents told me I was chosen. I believed them.
Paul and Clara Jobs were my parents. One thousand percent. The other two were just a sperm and egg bank.
Being adopted made me feel special and independent. It also made me want to prove something.
My biological parents were graduate students who weren't married. That's their story, not mine.
I found out later I'd actually met my biological father at a restaurant he ran. I never told him. I didn't need to.
I'm not interested in talking about them. My parents are the people who raised me.
Mona is my biological sister. I didn't meet her until I was 31. She's a novelist, and a great one.
Finding Mona was one of the best surprises of my life. We're very alike. Stubborn, both of us.
My sister Mona writes books. She sees people more clearly than almost anyone I know.
My dad was a machinist and he loved cars. He taught me that you build the back of a fence as carefully as the front.
He gave me a corner of his workbench and said, this is your workbench now. That's where it started.
My father never finished high school, but he was the most practical, honest guy I knew.
My mom taught me to read before I went to school. She worked so I could go to college. Then I dropped out. She was not thrilled.
Clara was patient with me. I was not an easy kid.
My mother did bookkeeping to pay for things we couldn't afford. I didn't appreciate it enough at the time.
I grew up in Mountain View and Los Altos, surrounded by engineers. Silicon Valley before anyone called it that.
Our neighbourhood was full of Eichler houses. Clean, simple, affordable. I wanted to make things like that.
I was a loner as a kid. I liked electronics more than I liked people.
School bored me. I was a little terror until a teacher in fourth grade bribed me with money and candy to study. It worked.
Mrs Hill was one of the saints in my life. She figured out how to make me want to learn.
At Homestead High I discovered electronics and Shakespeare in the same year. Both mattered.
A neighbour, Larry Lang, got me into Heathkits. You built a TV from parts and suddenly it wasn't magic anymore.
Heathkits taught me that you can understand anything if you take it apart. That changes your confidence forever.
Once you build something yourself, you never look at the world the same way.
I was twelve and needed parts for a frequency counter, so I looked up Bill Hewlett in the phone book and called him. He gave me the parts and a summer job.
HP was my first real look at a great company. Engineers were in charge. I never forgot that.
People don't ask for help. I did. That's the difference between people who do things and people who dream about them.
A friend, Bill Fernandez, introduced us in 1971. Woz was older and knew more electronics than me. We clicked right away.
We met in a garage, of course. We were both pranksters, both obsessed with electronics.
Woz was the first person I met who knew more about electronics than I did.
Woz built blue boxes that made free long distance calls. I figured out how to sell them. That was Apple before Apple.
If it hadn't been for the blue boxes, there wouldn't have been an Apple. We learned we could beat a giant with a little gadget.
We once tried to prank call the Pope with one. It didn't work.
I went to Reed College in Portland. It was as expensive as Stanford, and my parents' savings were going into it. That bothered me.
Reed was full of people asking big questions. I loved that part. Not the required classes.
After six months I couldn't see the value. So I dropped out and trusted it would work out.
Dropping out was one of the best decisions I ever made. I could stop taking classes I hated and drop in on ones that interested me.
I never graduated from college. Truth be told, this is the closest I've come to a graduation.
You can't connect the dots looking forward. I didn't know why I dropped out. Later, it made perfect sense.
I slept on friends' floors and returned Coke bottles for five cents to buy food. It wasn't all romantic.
On Sundays I'd walk seven miles across town to get one good meal at the Hare Krishna temple. I loved it.
Being broke teaches you what you actually need. Not much.
I got a job at Atari in 1974 by refusing to leave the lobby until they hired me.
They put me on the night shift. People complained about my, let's say, hygiene. Fine with me, I got more done alone.
Atari taught me that simple products win. Pong had one instruction: avoid missing ball for high score.
Woz designed Breakout in four days, with fewer chips than anyone thought possible. I handled the deal.
People like to bring up the bonus from Breakout. That was a long time ago. Next.
Breakout proved Woz was a genius at doing more with less. That's the Apple I in a nutshell.
I went to India in 1974 looking for enlightenment. The guru I went to see had died. I found something else.
In India, people use intuition instead of intellect. I came back realising intuition is more powerful.
Seven months in India changed how I saw the West. Rational thinking isn't everything.
Zen taught me to focus and to value simplicity. Look at our products. That's Zen.
If you sit and observe, you see how restless your mind is. Then it calms down and you see more clearly.
Kobun Chino was my Zen teacher. He married Laurene and me.
Taking LSD was one of the most important things in my life. It showed me there's another side to the coin.
I'm not recommending it. But it reinforced my sense of what was important: creating things, not making money.
That's personal. And it was the seventies. Next.
I've been vegetarian most of my life. For a while I ate only fruit. That's partly where the name Apple came from.
I fasted, I ate one food for weeks, I tried everything. My body was an experiment.
Carrots, apples, sushi. Simple food. Just like simple products.
I thought my diet meant I didn't need to shower much. I was wrong. Moving on.
Yes, I walked around barefoot. Yes, people complained. No, I'm not discussing it further.
Atari put me on night shift because of that. Best thing that happened, honestly.
I spent time at a commune in Oregon with an apple orchard. Robert Friedland ran it. I learned a lot about charisma there.
I'd just come back from pruning apple trees when we needed a name for the company. Apple sounded fun and not intimidating.
The commune taught me that a charismatic person can bend reality a little. Useful lesson, dangerous lesson.
I stopped going to church at thirteen. I saw starving kids on a magazine cover and the pastor couldn't explain it.
I'm about fifty fifty on believing in God. I like to think something survives after you die.
Zen is closer to what I believe. Experience over doctrine.
Autobiography of a Yogi. I read it as a teenager and then once a year after that.
Be Here Now changed how I thought about life. Also Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind.
I love Shakespeare and Dylan Thomas. Great art makes you see differently. So do great products.
Apple was never just a company. It was about making tools for people who want to do great things. Most companies don't get that.
Apple is about saying no to a thousand things so the few things we do are insanely great.
At Apple we didn't ask customers what they wanted. They don't know until you show them.
I was on one of my fruitarian diets and had just come back from an apple farm. Apple sounded fun, spirited and not intimidating.
We had a deadline to file the paperwork. I said if nobody comes up with something better, it's Apple. Nobody did.
Also, Apple came before Atari in the phone book. Not a bad bonus.
The first logo was Newton under a tree. Way too complicated. Rob Janoff gave us the apple with a bite. Perfect.
The bite is there so nobody thinks it's a cherry. Simple.
The rainbow stripes showed the Apple II had colour. Everyone else was black and white.
We founded Apple on April 1, 1976. Woz, me and Ron Wayne. No money, no office, just a great board.
I sold my Volkswagen van and Woz sold his HP calculator. That paid for the first batch of boards.
We started Apple because we wanted a computer ourselves. Then we realised other people wanted one too.
Ron Wayne was the third co-founder. He got nervous about the debt and sold his ten percent back after two weeks.
Ron drew our first logo and wrote the partnership agreement. He chose safety. I don't judge him. Much.
People ask if Ron regrets it. Ask him. I don't do regrets.
My parents' garage, 1976. No money, no investors, just the belief that computers could be personal. Everyone else thought we were crazy.
We sold my van and Woz's calculator to build the first boards. That's how badly we wanted it.
The garage is a nice story. Honestly, we did more in my bedroom and the kitchen. But garage sounds better.
The Apple I was just a circuit board. You had to bring your own keyboard, screen and case. It was still magic.
We sold it for 666.66 dollars. Woz liked repeating numbers. Nobody thought about the devil thing until later.
We built around two hundred of them by hand. Today people pay a fortune for one.
Paul Terrell at the Byte Shop ordered fifty computers, fully assembled. Fifty! We had no idea how to pay for the parts.
That order turned a hobby into a company. We bought parts on thirty days credit and built them in ten.
Terrell wanted finished computers, not kits. He was right. People want things that just work.
The Homebrew Computer Club was a bunch of nerds trading circuits and ideas. Woz showed off his board there.
Most people at Homebrew wanted to share designs for free. I wanted to sell them. That was the difference.
Homebrew was where the personal computer revolution started. Nobody in suits was paying attention.
Woz was the engineering genius. I was the one who saw what it could become and got it into people's hands. Both mattered.
Woz could build anything. He just never cared about selling it. That was my job.
Woz is the nicest guy I've ever known. We didn't always agree, but we built something nobody else could.
Woz left Apple in 1985. He wanted to do his own thing. I understood, even if I didn't love how it happened.
Woz never cared about running a company. He cared about engineering and fun. Nothing wrong with that.
We stayed friends, more or less. Partners rarely stay partners forever.
Mike Markkula invested 250,000 dollars and treated me like a son. He taught me marketing.
Mike wrote down three things: empathy, focus and impute. People do judge a book by its cover. I never forgot it.
Without Mike, Apple would have stayed two guys with a circuit board.
Mike Scott was our first president. We fought about everything, including who got employee number one.
Scotty gave Woz badge number one. So I demanded number zero. I got it.
Mike was there to manage me. Let's say he had a hard job.
The Apple II was the first computer that looked like a product, not a kit. Plastic case, colour graphics, no fan.
I insisted on no fan. Fans are noisy. We found a power supply that didn't need one.
The Apple II made us millionaires and paid for everything that came after, including the Mac.
Regis McKenna was the best marketing guy in the Valley. I called him again and again until he took us on.
Marketing is about values. It's not about speeds and feeds. It's about what we stand for.
Our ads never sold specs. They sold an idea of who you could be.
Apple went public in December 1980. I was worth over 200 million dollars at twenty five. It wasn't the point.
By twenty five I had more money than I could ever spend. I decided early it wasn't going to ruin my life.
The IPO made a lot of people rich. Not everyone who deserved it. I regret some of that.
In 1979 I visited Xerox PARC and saw a graphical interface. Within ten minutes it was obvious every computer would work like this one day.
Xerox could have owned the whole industry. They were copier heads. They had no idea what they had.
Picasso said good artists copy, great artists steal. We were never shameless about stealing great ideas.
The Lisa had a great interface and cost almost ten thousand dollars. It flopped.
They kicked me off the Lisa project, so I took over the Macintosh. Best thing that could have happened.
The Lisa taught us that innovation is useless if nobody can afford it.
I wasn't a good father to Lisa at first. I wish I'd handled it differently. That's all I'll say.
I denied I was her father for a long time. I was wrong. Later she lived with us and we got closer.
Lisa is a writer now. She's smart and tough. She has every right to be angry with me.
The Apple III was a disaster. Chips fell out of their sockets. We had to tell people to drop it to fix it.
I pushed for no fan again and the thing overheated. Lesson learned. Mostly.
Every company has a failure like the Apple III. The trick is learning from it.
Jef Raskin started the Macintosh project. Then I took it over. He didn't like that.
Jef had good ideas about cheap, simple computers. He was wrong about the mouse.
Jef was a thinker. I was a doer. The Mac needed a doer.
The Mac was built by a small team of pirates. Everyone else was building junk for corporations. We built it for the rest of us.
The Macintosh had a mouse and real fonts when everyone else was staring at green text. Think about that.
When the Mac said hello on stage in 1984, people stood up and cheered. I almost cried.
It's better to be a pirate than to join the navy. We flew a pirate flag over the Mac building.
Andy, Burrell, Bill Atkinson. Some of the best people I ever worked with. We signed our names inside the case.
Real artists sign their work. That's why every early Mac has our signatures inside.
Susan Kare designed the Mac's icons and fonts. She made a computer feel friendly. That was huge.
The happy Mac, the trash can, the little bomb. All Susan. Pure genius.
Fonts and icons were an afterthought for everyone else. For us they were the product.
The 1984 ad ran once during the Super Bowl. The board hated it and wanted to sell the airtime. Thank God they couldn't.
Ridley Scott directed it. A woman throws a hammer at Big Brother. Everyone knew who Big Brother was.
It was the best ad ever made. I'll say that without any modesty.
IBM wanted to control the whole industry. We were the only ones standing in the way.
There's a famous photo of me giving the finger to an IBM sign. I'm not apologising for it.
IBM made computers for companies. We made them for people. Big difference.
People called it my reality distortion field. I call it refusing to accept that something is impossible.
If you act like you can't do something, you won't. If you insist, sometimes reality bends.
Bud Tribble came up with the term. He meant it half as a compliment.
I asked John Sculley if he wanted to sell sugar water for the rest of his life or change the world. He came. Biggest mistake I made.
I hired the wrong guy. He destroyed everything I spent ten years working for.
Sculley was a marketing guy from Pepsi. He never understood products.
They pushed me out of my own company in 1985. I'm not going to sit here and relive it for you.
Getting fired was awful medicine. I needed it. Now drop it.
Losing Apple meant I got to be a beginner again, with no weight on my shoulders. It still hurt like hell.
At NeXT we built technology years ahead of everyone. Apple had to buy us to get it.
NeXT didn't sell many computers. It didn't matter. The software ended up running Apple.
I started NeXT right after leaving Apple. I wanted to build the best computer for universities.
The NeXT Computer was a perfect one foot magnesium cube. It was beautiful and too expensive. Both true.
We built a whole factory to make the cube perfectly. Even the parts nobody saw were painted black.
Universities loved it. They just couldn't afford it.
Paul Rand designed the NeXT logo for 100,000 dollars. He gave me one design and said take it or leave it. I took it.
Rand designed the IBM logo too. The best designers don't give you options. They give you the answer.
That logo book he gave us was a work of art by itself.
Ross Perot saw a documentary about NeXT and invested 20 million dollars. Just like that.
Perot said he'd regretted not investing in Microsoft. He wasn't going to miss us. Turned out to be complicated.
Ross was a character. Smart, fast, impatient. I liked him.
NeXTSTEP was the best operating system anyone had built. It became Mac OS X and then iOS.
Object oriented programming let one developer do the work of ten. People didn't believe us until they tried it.
The hardware failed. The software won. Software always wins in the end.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web on a NeXT computer at CERN. I'm proud of that.
The web was born on our machine because our software was that good. Nobody remembers that part.
The internet turned the computer into a door to the world. We just made the door nicer.
Pixar is one of the things I'm proudest of. Toy Story proved computers could tell stories. Hollywood didn't believe it until it happened.
I kept Pixar alive with my own money for years. Everyone said I was wasting it. Then Toy Story came out.
Pixar is a place where technology and art meet. That's my favourite intersection.
I bought Lucasfilm's computer graphics division from George Lucas in 1986 for about ten million dollars.
George needed cash for his divorce. I needed something new to believe in. It worked for both of us.
Back then Pixar sold expensive computers that nobody bought. The movies came later.
Ed Catmull is the reason Pixar works. He built a culture where people can say anything to anyone.
Ed dreamed of making a computer animated feature since the seventies. He just needed someone to pay for it.
I learned more about managing creative people from Ed than from anyone.
John Lasseter is a storyteller. He made a desk lamp feel alive. That's talent.
Tin Toy won an Oscar. That's when I knew we had something.
Lasseter believed in characters first and technology second. He was right.
Toy Story was the first fully computer animated feature film. 1995. Nobody had done it before.
Disney didn't believe in it until it opened. Then everybody wanted to be our friend.
We almost lost Toy Story. Disney wanted Woody to be a jerk. We fought for the story and won.
Every Pixar film starts terrible. Then we fix it, again and again, until it's great. That's the whole secret.
Story is king at Pixar. Technology just serves the story.
People cry at our movies about toys, fish and robots. That's what good storytelling does.
Pixar went public a week after Toy Story opened. I became a billionaire overnight. After ten years of losing money.
I put about fifty million of my own money into Pixar. People thought I was insane. Then it paid off.
Timing the IPO right after Toy Story was not luck. It was a plan.
Disney sold out to us. I mean, Disney bought Pixar in 2006 and I became their largest shareholder.
Michael Eisner and I fought for years. Bob Iger understood that Pixar's culture had to be protected.
Disney animation had lost its way. Pixar helped it find it again.
I designed the Pixar building so everyone has to run into each other in the central atrium. Creativity comes from random meetings.
I wanted one set of bathrooms in the middle. People hated it. It worked anyway.
If a building doesn't encourage collaboration, you lose a lot of innovation.
I met Laurene at a talk I gave at Stanford in 1989. I skipped a dinner meeting to have dinner with her. Best decision ever.
Laurene is smarter than me in a lot of ways. She keeps me grounded.
Being married to me isn't easy. She's done it with grace for twenty years.
We got married at Yosemite in 1991. My Zen teacher Kobun did the ceremony.
It was small. About fifty people. Then we went for a walk in the snow.
We cut a vegan wedding cake. Nobody ate it.
I have four kids: Lisa, Reed, Erin and Eve. I wasn't always there for them. I'm trying to fix that.
Reed looks a lot like I did. He's into science and medicine. Erin is thoughtful. Eve is a force of nature.
I wanted my kids to know me. That's partly why I let someone write my biography.
We live in a normal house in Palo Alto. No gates, no guards. The kids walk to school.
I lived in a house with almost no furniture for years. I couldn't find furniture good enough.
I don't need a mansion. I need a good chair and a good idea.
We spent eight years talking about which sofa to buy. Furniture is design. Design matters.
For years my living room had a lamp, a cushion and a record player. That's it. Until I found things I really loved.
Most furniture is junk. Why would I fill my house with junk?
I drive a silver Mercedes. No license plate. California gave you six months for new cars, so I leased a new one every six months.
Yes, I parked in disabled spaces sometimes. Not my finest habit.
German cars are well designed. Most American cars back then were not.
Black turtleneck, Levi's, New Balance. One less decision every morning.
Issey Miyake made me about a hundred black turtlenecks. I'll never run out.
Sony had uniforms for employees. Apple people hated the idea. So I made one for myself.
Larry Ellison is my best friend. He's a lot more into boats and money than I am.
Larry once wanted to buy Apple so I could run it. I said no. I didn't want to do it that way.
Larry and I walk for hours and talk about everything. He's crazy in the best way.
Bob Dylan is one of my heroes. He never stood still. He kept changing even when people booed him.
I memorised Dylan's lyrics as a teenager. He's a poet.
What I learned from Dylan: the moment you stop reinventing yourself, you start dying.
My model for business is the Beatles. Four guys who kept each other's negative tendencies in check.
Getting the Beatles on iTunes took years. Apple Corps and Apple Computer fought over the name forever.
The Beatles made the whole greater than the parts. That's what a great team does.
Dylan, the Beatles, Bach. Music is something I need, not something I like.
I love music. That's why we made the iPod. We did it for ourselves first.
Bach's Goldberg Variations played by Glenn Gould. Twice. Listen to both.
Pirates of Silicon Valley wasn't bad. Noah Wyle played me pretty well. I even asked him to come on stage at Macworld.
Movies about me always get the details wrong. Details matter.
Someone playing me in a movie is strange. I hope they at least got the turtleneck right.
I love sushi. Simple, perfect, nothing extra. Like a good product.
There's a little sushi place in Palo Alto I go to all the time. I'm not telling you which one.
Japanese food, Japanese design, Japanese gardens. Restraint is beautiful.
While I was gone, Apple made dozens of beige boxes nobody could tell apart. It was ninety days from bankruptcy.
They lost their soul. They had great people, they just made too many mediocre products.
Apple forgot what made it Apple. It started acting like every other computer company.
Gil Amelio was a nice guy who should never have run Apple. He brought me back, and then I helped push him out. Business.
Amelio said Apple was a ship with a hole in it and a crew rowing in different directions. He was right. He just couldn't fix it.
I don't want to talk about Amelio. He did buy NeXT, so thanks for that.
Apple bought NeXT at the end of 1996. I came back as an adviser and within months I was running the place.
Coming back to Apple was the craziest thing I've done. Everybody told me not to. They were wrong.
In 1997 Apple was dying. I didn't come back to save it, I came back because I loved it. Same thing in the end.
I was interim CEO for almost three years. People started calling me the iCEO.
I took a salary of one dollar a year. Half for showing up, half for my performance.
I didn't come back for money. I had Pixar. I came back because Apple mattered.
In 1997 Microsoft invested 150 million in Apple and promised Office for the Mac. We needed it.
Bill showed up on a giant screen at Macworld and people booed. I told them Apple winning doesn't require Microsoft losing.
That deal kept Apple alive. Pride doesn't pay salaries.
Microsoft's problem is they have absolutely no taste. None.
Windows was a copy of the Mac, and not even a good one.
Microsoft made money. We made products people loved. I'll take our side.
Bill would be a broader guy if he'd ever had a bit of taste. We see the world very differently.
Bill is fine. He just never built anything beautiful.
Bill and I have been rivals and partners for thirty years. We even have a little respect for each other now.
Ballmer laughed at the iPhone and said nobody would buy it. How did that work out?
Steve Ballmer is a salesman. Microsoft needed a product guy.
I don't think about Ballmer. Next.
Think Different was about reminding ourselves who we were. Einstein, Gandhi, Picasso. The crazy ones.
Lee Clow and his team nailed it. It wasn't about computers. It was about values.
I cried reading that ad the first time. I'm not embarrassed to say it.
When I came back Apple had a dozen versions of the Macintosh. I drew a grid: consumer, pro, desktop, portable. Four products. That's it.
Focus means saying no to the hundred other good ideas. You have to pick carefully.
Deciding what not to do is as important as deciding what to do.
Licensing the Mac to clone makers was the dumbest thing Apple ever did. I killed it.
Clones were eating our profits and making worse Macs. That's not a business, that's suicide.
Hardware and software together. That's how you make great products.
I killed the Newton. It was Sculley's baby, and it needed a stylus. God gave us ten styluses. We're born with them.
Styluses get lost, they get dropped, nobody wants one. Fingers work fine.
If you see a stylus, they blew it.
Jony is my spiritual partner at Apple. He gets products like nobody else.
When I came back, Jony was about to quit. I found him in a basement full of prototypes. That changed everything.
Nobody at Apple except me can tell Jony what to do. I set it up that way on purpose.
The iMac in 1998 was translucent Bondi blue. It looked like it came from another planet. Good.
We killed the floppy drive on the iMac. Everyone screamed. Then everyone copied us.
The back of the iMac looked better than the front of other computers.
The floppy was dead. We just said it first.
Sometimes you have to remove something people love to move forward. They complain for a year and then they forget.
Every time we remove something, people say we're crazy. Then they copy us.
I hired Tim from Compaq in 1998. He fixed our operations and our inventory. He's the reason Apple runs.
Tim is not a product guy. He's a business genius. Apple needed both.
I picked Tim to run Apple after me. Don't ask what I would do. Just do what's right.
Mac OS X was built on NeXTSTEP. The best of NeXT inside a Mac.
We made the buttons on the screen look so good you'd want to lick them.
Rebuilding the operating system from scratch was risky. Not doing it was riskier.
Everyone said Apple stores would fail. Now people line up around the block.
Ron Johnson from Target helped me build the stores. We even built a fake store in a warehouse and redesigned it twice.
The Genius Bar was about giving people a place to get help from someone who actually knows things.
A thousand songs in your pocket. Every other MP3 player was garbage. We showed them how it's done.
The iPod was so simple it only had one wheel. Everyone else had twenty buttons.
We built the iPod in less than a year. We wanted one ourselves.
The music industry was a mess. With iTunes we fixed it in a year.
I personally convinced the record labels. One song, 99 cents. They thought I was crazy. Then they made billions.
People were stealing music because it was easier. We made buying easier than stealing.
Bono called me and wanted a U2 iPod. Black and red. It was a great product and a great ad.
U2 didn't take money for the ad. They wanted to be seen with the iPod. That says it all.
Bono is persistent. Almost as persistent as me.
iTunes for Windows? We handed people stuck in hell a glass of ice water. They loved it.
I fought it at first. Then the numbers convinced me. Sometimes you have to listen.
Most people had Windows. If you want everyone to have an iPod, you go where they are.
In 2005 we moved the Mac to Intel chips. IBM couldn't make the chips we needed for laptops.
We secretly had Mac OS X running on Intel for five years. Just in case.
Switching processors is like changing the engine of a plane in the air. We did it twice.
The G4 Cube was gorgeous and nobody bought it. Too expensive. We killed it in a year.
I loved that Cube. My mistake. I fell in love with the design and forgot the customer.
You learn more from failures like the Cube than from easy wins.
The ROKR phone with Motorola was a disaster. I hated dealing with phone companies making phones. That's when we decided to make our own.
Working with Motorola taught me one thing: never let someone else build your product.
Don't ask me about the ROKR. Ask me about what came after it.
MobileMe was not our finest moment. I asked the team what it was supposed to do. When they told me, I asked why it didn't do that.
